contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: William the Conqueror was duke of Normandy and, after 1066, king of England. His victory at the Battle of Hastings over Harold Godwinson transformed England, tied it more closely to Normandy and northern France, and reshaped aristocratic landholding, castles, language, law, and royal government.

Born illegitimate at Falaise, William survived a dangerous Norman childhood before becoming one of the most consequential rulers in medieval Europe. He died at Rouen in 1087 after injury and illness, leaving England and Normandy to different heirs and a legacy of conquest that remained deeply contested.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: William was born around 1028 at Falaise in the Duchy of Normandy, the son of Duke Robert I and Herleva. His illegitimacy made his early position vulnerable, especially after he inherited Normandy as a child.

Norman politics were violent, and William survived rebellion, aristocratic rivalries, and threats to his authority before establishing himself as duke. That hard apprenticeship shaped his later reliance on castles, loyal magnates, and disciplined military force.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: William the Conqueror's character was remembered through severity and command. Norman sources such as William of Poitiers emphasised his legitimacy, discipline, and piety, while English memory — and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle — preserved the violence of conquest, dispossession, and above all the Harrying of the North, when he devastated whole regions to break resistance. The same chronicle that records his harshness also credits him with a fierce sense of order: "so stern and hot" a man that no one dared act against his will.

His personality should not be reduced to cruelty alone. He was politically patient, careful with claims of law and inheritance, and capable of binding the Norman aristocracy to a long, disciplined project of occupation. He was personally pious in the conventional manner of his age, founding Battle Abbey on the site of Hastings, yet entirely willing to use terror as an instrument of rule when opposition hardened.

Contemporaries also noted his physical formidableness and his growing corpulence in later life, the subject of a mocking jest by the king of France that William answered with a punitive campaign. The anecdote, whatever its truth, fits the remembered man: proud, unforgiving of insult, and relentless once provoked.

contentSections.title: As duke of Normandy and king of England
paragraphs: As duke of Normandy, William built a powerful cross-Channel principality and claimed that Edward the Confessor had promised him the English throne. After Harold Godwinson became king in 1066, William invaded England and won the Battle of Hastings.

As king of England, he rewarded Norman followers, built castles, suppressed revolts, and ordered the Domesday survey. His rule joined England to Norman and French politics while permanently altering the English aristocracy.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died at Rouen in 1087 after injury or illness connected to his campaign in the Vexin.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: William is remembered as the ruler who redirected English history through conquest. His regime transformed landholding, church leadership, castle building, legal record keeping, and aristocratic culture.
His reputation is still contested: to some traditions he was a founder of a stronger monarchy, while to others he was an invader whose conquest brought dispossession and violence.

timeline.title: Born
timeline.description: William was born at Falaise as the illegitimate son of Duke Robert I of Normandy, a background that shaped his contested early rule.

timeline.title: Becomes Duke of Normandy
timeline.description: Inherits Normandy as a child after Robert I dies.

timeline.title: Secures Normandy after Val-es-Dunes
timeline.description: Defeats rebel Norman barons with support from King Henry I of France.

timeline.title: Wins the Battle of Hastings
timeline.description: Defeats Harold Godwinson and opens the Norman conquest of England.

timeline.title: Crowned king of England
timeline.description: Crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day.

timeline.title: Orders the Domesday survey
timeline.description: Commissions a kingdom-wide record of landholding and obligations.

timeline.title: Died
timeline.description: Dies after injury and illness while campaigning in France.
